title: JESUS WAS ASKED ABOUT DIVORCE—AND HIS ANSWER WENT ALL THE WAY BACK TO MALE, FEMALE, ONE FLESH, AND GOD
paragraphs: JESUS WAS ASKED ABOUT DIVORCE—AND HIS ANSWER WENT ALL THE WAY BACK TO MALE, FEMALE, ONE FLESH, AND GOD
They asked Jesus when a marriage could be broken.
Jesus answered by reminding them what marriage was before human hearts started breaking it.
And if you read His words slowly enough, you may discover that Matthew 19 is not merely a passage about divorce.
It is a confrontation with the human heart.
“Have ye not read…?”
That was how Jesus began.
Not with popular opinion.
Not with cultural trends.
Not with whatever happened to be socially convenient.
Not even with the pain of human failure as the definition of what marriage was supposed to be.
He took them backward.
Past their arguments.
Past their loopholes.
Past their legal debates.
Past Moses.
All the way back to creation.
And what Jesus said there is almost impossible to misunderstand without first deciding that we do not want to hear it.
The question brought to Him concerned divorce, but His answer began with a Creator.
Matthew records His words in Greek:
“ὁ κτίσας ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησεν αὐτούς”
In plain English:
“The One who created them from the beginning made them male and female.”
ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ.
Arsen kai thēly.
Male and female.
Jesus was reaching directly back to Genesis.
He did not treat the creation account as an embarrassing relic that enlightened people needed to outgrow. He appealed to it as the foundation from which His hearers should understand marriage.
That matters.
But keep reading, because Jesus was not finished.
He continued:
“Ἕνεκα τούτου καταλείψει ἄνθρωπος τὸν πατέρα καὶ τὴν μητέρα καὶ κολληθήσεται τῇ γυναικὶ αὐτοῦ…”
“For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife…”
Then:
“καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν”
“And the two shall become one flesh.”
Not merely two people sharing a house.
Not merely two names printed on a certificate.
Not merely two people who feel intensely about each other today and reserve the right to disappear when those feelings become difficult tomorrow.
One flesh.
Then Jesus takes the truth even deeper:
“ὥστε οὐκέτι εἰσὶν δύο ἀλλὰ σὰρξ μία.”
“So they are no longer two, but one flesh.”
And then comes the sentence that should make every married person, every person considering marriage, every pastor performing a wedding, and every Christian discussing marriage stop for a moment:
“ὃ οὖν ὁ θεὸς συνέζευξεν ἄνθρωπος μὴ χωριζέτω.”
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Read those words again.
God has joined.
That is the part our generation can easily forget.
Marriage, in Jesus’ teaching, is not merely something two people manufacture for themselves.
God is not standing outside the ceremony as a distant spectator.
Jesus places God Himself at the center.
The Greek verb translated “joined together” is συνέζευξεν—synezeuxen—carrying the sense of joining or yoking together.
Suddenly the question changes.
Instead of merely asking, “What do I want from this marriage?”
we are forced to ask:
“What has God joined?”
Instead of only asking, “Am I still happy?”
another question enters the room:
“Am I being faithful?”
Instead of treating marriage as nothing more than a contract whose terms survive only while both parties remain satisfied, Scripture presents something far weightier.
And here we need to be careful with the Bible.
Matthew 19:4–6 itself does not contain the Greek word for “covenant.”
Jesus speaks there about creation, male and female, leaving father and mother, becoming one flesh, and what God has joined together.
But elsewhere Scripture explicitly describes marriage with covenant language.
Malachi 2:14 contains these haunting Hebrew words:
“וְאֵשֶׁת בְּרִיתֶךָ”
ve’eshet beritekha—
“the wife of your covenant.”
The Hebrew word בְּרִית—berit—means covenant.
And notice the surrounding thought.
God says that He has been witness between a husband and “the wife of your youth.”
Think about that.
God witnessed it.
That young couple may have thought only family and friends were watching.
God was watching.
The promises mattered.
The faithfulness mattered.
The tears mattered.
The betrayal mattered.
The covenant mattered.
And maybe this is where this article stops being theological information and starts becoming painfully personal.
Because some of you reading this once stood across from someone with trembling hands and shining eyes and made promises you genuinely believed you would keep.
You had no idea how difficult life could become.
You had not yet met the exhausted version of each other.
The financially stressed version.
The grieving version.
The disappointed version.
The aging version.
The wounded version.
The version that stopped communicating well.
The version carrying childhood scars into adult arguments.
The version that could hurt you with one sentence because they knew exactly where your heart was tender.
You promised before you knew.
And then life taught you what promises cost.
Maybe your marriage is strong today.
Thank God.
Protect it.
Feed it.
Pray over it.
Do not become careless merely because you have survived this far.
The strongest-looking walls can develop cracks when nobody is watching.
Maybe your marriage is hanging by a thread.
Maybe you sleep beside someone who feels a thousand miles away.
Maybe conversation has become logistics.
Bills.
Children.
Schedules.
Work.
Groceries.
Appointments.
Then silence.
Maybe there was betrayal.
Maybe there were words that cannot be unsaid.
Maybe affection slowly died under years of unresolved resentment.
Maybe you are reading an article about marriage while quietly wondering whether yours can still be resurrected.
And perhaps nobody knows.
You smile at church.
You upload the family photograph.
You answer, “We’re doing fine.”
But God knows what happens after the door closes.
Please hear something important.
The holiness of marriage must never be used as a weapon to pretend sin does not exist.

Jesus Himself continues the discussion beyond verses 4–6 and addresses sexual immorality in Matthew 19:9. Paul later addresses situations involving an unbelieving spouse who abandons the marriage in 1 Corinthians 7:15.
So biblical faithfulness requires more than shouting, “God hates divorce,” at wounded people and walking away.
God also hates treachery.
He cares about truth.
He cares about faithfulness.
He cares about the wounded.
He cares about holiness.
He cares about what happens behind closed doors.

And a person facing abuse or immediate danger should not interpret “one flesh” as a command to remain physically exposed to violence. Seeking safety, wise pastoral counsel, appropriate professional help, and lawful protection is not the same thing as treating marriage casually.
Scripture should never be manipulated into becoming camouflage for evil.
But neither should human failure be allowed to rewrite God’s design.
That tension matters.
Grace does not call evil good.
Truth does not require us to become cruel.
Jesus somehow holds both perfectly.
And perhaps that is because Jesus did not come merely to win debates.
He came to save sinners.
Which means Matthew 19 eventually points beyond the marriage argument and directly toward us.
Because if we are going to talk about covenant faithfulness, sooner or later every one of us has to confront an uncomfortable reality:
We have all been unfaithful to God.
Maybe not in the same ways.
But every one of us has sinned.
Every one of us has wanted God's gifts while resisting God's authority.
Every one of us has crossed lines.
Every one of us has carried something into the darkness hoping heaven would not mention it.
Pride.
Lust.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Adultery.
Emotional affairs.
Secret messages.
Selfishness.
Manipulation.
Unforgiveness.
Deception.
A wandering imagination.
A hardened heart.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody found the messages.
Maybe nobody discovered the browser history.
Maybe nobody knows what happened on that trip.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been imagining.
Maybe your reputation survived.
But surviving exposure is not the same thing as being clean.
Jesus did not come merely to improve our reputation.
He came to redeem us.
That is why the Gospel is so much more shocking than religious people sometimes make it sound.
Jesus knows the entire story.
And He still calls sinners to come.
Not to remain in sin.
Not to rename sin.
Not to justify sin.
Not to build an identity around rebellion.
To repent.
To believe.
To be forgiven.
To be changed.
The cross is where God's refusal to call sin harmless and God's willingness to forgive sinners meet.
Jesus Christ did not bleed because sin was insignificant.
He bled because sin was deadly.
And He rose because death would not have the final word.
Maybe you have already destroyed something precious.
Maybe you were the unfaithful spouse.
Maybe your selfishness poisoned the home.
Maybe you walked away.
Maybe you were the one abandoned.
Maybe somebody else's sin shattered the future you thought you had.
Maybe you are divorced and still carrying shame every time marriage is preached.
Maybe you remarried and have spent years wondering whether God only tolerates you from a distance.
Maybe you are single and this passage exposes compromises you have already begun making before marriage ever enters the picture.
Whatever brought you here, do not turn Matthew 19 into stones to throw at everybody else.
First allow the words of Jesus to search you.
“Have ye not read…?”
That question still reaches us.
Have we read what God said?
Not merely what our culture says.
Not merely what our pain says.
Not merely what our desires say.
Not merely what the internet says.
What did God say?
Jesus takes us back to the beginning because sometimes the only way to understand what has become broken is to remember what it was created to be.
Male and female.
A man leaving father and mother.
Joined to his wife.
Two becoming one flesh.
God joining.
Human beings warned not to tear apart what God has joined.
And yet even here, the final message cannot simply be, “Try harder.”
Because broken sinners cannot save themselves through stronger vows.
We need Christ.
The husband who has failed needs Christ.
The wife drowning in bitterness needs Christ.
The single person fighting sexual temptation needs Christ.
The divorced person carrying regret needs Christ.
The betrayed spouse trying to breathe again needs Christ.
The person secretly considering an affair needs Christ.
The person who already crossed the line needs Christ.
The religious person congratulating himself because his sins look more respectable needs Christ.
All of us do.
And when Christ enters the ruins, grace does not pretend the ruins never happened.
Grace begins rebuilding people inside them.
Repentance may require confession.
It may require ending the affair.
Deleting the number.
Breaking the secret connection.
Telling the truth.
Seeking counsel.
Accepting accountability.
Learning how to apologize without excuses.
Learning how to forgive without pretending wounds were harmless.
Learning how to become trustworthy again.
Sometimes reconciliation is a long road.
Sometimes consequences remain even after forgiveness.
Grace is not a time machine.
But grace means your worst chapter does not have to become the title of your entire life.
Peter denied Jesus and was restored.
The woman caught in adultery encountered mercy alongside the call to leave sin.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history, yet Jesus deliberately met her at the well.
The cross itself stands as God's declaration that sinners can be redeemed at a cost none of us could pay.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to these words:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting God's definition of righteousness.
By rewriting sinners.
He changes hearts.
He forgives guilt.
He breaks chains.
He restores what sin has devastated.
He teaches the proud to kneel.
He teaches the unfaithful to become faithful.
He teaches wounded people that their wound is not their identity.
He teaches sinners that repentance is not the doorway into humiliation.
It is the doorway home.
Maybe that is why you found this article today.
Not so you can send it angrily to your spouse.
Not so you can use Matthew 19 to win an argument on Facebook.
Maybe God wants you to become quiet enough to ask:
“Jesus, what are You saying to me?”
If something hidden has been exposed in your heart, do not run from Christ.
Run to Him.
If you need forgiveness, ask Him.
If repentance requires action, take it.
If your marriage needs help, stop protecting appearances while the relationship dies privately.
If you have wounded your spouse, humility is more powerful than another excuse.
If you have been wounded, know that seeking wise help does not make you faithless.
If you are single, decide now that God's design will matter more than cultural pressure when you eventually choose whom and how you love.
If conviction uncovered something you have been hiding, comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
If your marriage desperately needs prayer, comment, “Pray for us.”
If you are wounded but still trusting Christ, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
If you are fighting for faithfulness when giving up feels easier, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
And if you cannot explain everything publicly, simply write, “Jesus knows.”
Let somebody praying through these comments know they are not the only believer fighting battles behind a smile.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
Somebody may be sitting alone tonight convinced their failure has placed them beyond grace.
Somebody may be preparing to make a decision they will spend years wishing they could reverse.
Somebody may never enter a church building this week but may read something you were brave enough to put on your profile.
Not merely because you agree with it today.
He reminded them how God intended it to begin.
It never will.
Salvation is God's gift in Jesus Christ, received by grace through faith, not purchased through financial support.
Give freely.
Give prayerfully.
Give because you believe biblical truth should keep reaching people.
That support helps keep the mission moving.
You may not be able to preach to thousands.
But you can press “Share.”
And God can take truth farther than you can see.
Stay close to Scripture.
Stay close to conviction.
Stay close to grace.
Most importantly, stay close to Jesus.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Forgiveness cannot be purchased.
Christ already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Your money does not save you.
Jesus does.
Christ demonstrated God's love at the cross.
So pray.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Seek help where wisdom demands help.
Fight for faithfulness.
Speak truth with grace.
Save what you may need again.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody thinks their scandal is the end of their story.
Maybe it was adultery.
Maybe betrayal.
Maybe divorce.
Maybe secret sin.
Maybe years of pretending.
Maybe a marriage hanging by its final thread.
And into that wreckage Jesus Christ still walks with truth in His mouth, scars in His hands, and grace for repentant sinners.
He does not rewrite truth to accommodate our scandal.
He rewrites us by grace.
Remember that when your past whispers your name like a sentence:
Your scandal may explain the chapter you survived, but when Jesus takes hold of the story, your scandal does not get to write the ending.
